To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

countercurrent exchange in a system consisting of descending and ascending vasa rectas and descending limbs of Henle's loop can be modeled by solving a system of nonlinear equations that are derived from mass balances.
the countercurrent exchange system of the inner medulla is a passive system that can generate a large increase in solute concentrations toward the papilliae.
countercurrent exchangers with passive transport and decreasing source fluxes can yield solute concentrations that increase monotonically.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the modeling of transport processes in the inner medullary vasa recta-descending limb system.
the development of mathematical models of renal countercurrent exchanger systems, and with the use of these models to simulate transport processes within these systems.
a mathematical analysis of the countercurrent exchanger, the vasa recta descending limb system, and its role in the renal concentrating mechanism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
countercurrent multiplication is not a necessary condition for the formation of the high solute concentrations in the papilla.
the vasa recta-descending limb countercurrent exchanger is capable of generating the steep salt and urea gradients observed in the inner renal cortex.

a countercurrent exchange system can be constructed that is capable of generating a high osmolarity in the interstitial space of the inner medulla and that the countercurrent mechanism can operate in the absence of active transport processes in the exchanger.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the countercurrent exchanger in the inner medullary vasa recta-descending limb system can produce a concentration gradient for salt and urea, and a volume flow rate gradient for salt, urea, and water, even though all transport processes within this exchanger are passive, and all source fluxes decrease toward the papillia.
a countercurrent exchanger can generate large concentration differences in a system of passive transport processes if the source fluxes decrease toward the papillas.
the vasa recta-desending limb countercurrent exchanger can produce a concentration polarization of salt in the descending vasa rectas even if the source fluxes are monotonically decreasing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a model of countercurent exchange need not include any active transport processes to yield the observed salt and urea concentration gradients in the inner medullary interstitium.
the vasa recta-descending limb exchanger can generate a large concentration gradient of solutes in the inner medullary region.
a model that includes passive diffusion, active transport, and countercurrent exchange can explain how the kidney concentrates solutes in the inner medullary interstitium.
